manifest.title: Linear Programming: Duality, Certificates, and Polynomial-Time Optimization

inputs.abstract:
This submission treats finite real linear programs in the form
$\max\{c^T x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}$ and their nonnegative-multiplier duals.
The mathematical concepts include weak and strong duality, complementary
slackness, primal attainment, Farkas' alternative, and certificates of
unboundedness. Exact rational certificates cover optimality, infeasibility,
and unboundedness of rational programs optimized over real variables.
The elimination and Farkas proofs adapt Jyotirmoy Bhattacharya's
MIT-licensed [farkas_lean](https://github.com/jmoy/farkas_lean) formalization.

The algorithmic scope is one uniform exact polynomial-time solver, measured
in the binary size of the rational input and using the registered word-RAM
model of [lax-808846](https://laxarchive.org/lax-808846/) through the
polynomial-time predicate of [lax-759944](https://laxarchive.org/lax-759944/).
The solver returns the encoding of the certificate that validates its answer.
Polynomial-size certificate existence is proved independently. The solver
uses the rational ellipsoid method and exact certificate recovery.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.RationalFeasibility
import Lax109476.StrongDuality
import Lax109476.RecessionExistence

/-!
---
title: Exact rational certificates exist for all linear-programming outcomes
type: theorem
---
Every rational linear program has an exact rational certificate: a matching
primal–dual pair, nonnegative Farkas multipliers, or a feasible point and
an improving recession direction.

# Formalization notes

The certificate conditions are checked in the rationals and describe
optimization over real variables. This is an existence theorem independent
of polynomial-time solvability. It does not assert a size or runtime bound.
-/

namespace Lax109476.CertificateExistence

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.RationalCertificates

/-- Every rational coefficient input has an exact valid outcome certificate. -/
axiom exists_valid_certificate :
  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℚ m n), ∃ certificate : Certificate m n,
    IsValidCertificate P certificate

end Lax109476.CertificateExistence

statements.signature:
exists_valid_certificate : ∀ (m n : Nat) (P : Lax109476.LinearProgram.Program Rat m n),
  Exists fun certificate => Lax109476.RationalCertificates.IsValidCertificate P certificate
statements.doc: Every rational coefficient input has an exact valid outcome certificate.

concepts.title: Soundness of exact rational LP certificates
concepts.description:
Every valid rational certificate establishes its claimed outcome for the
linear program over real variables. Matching primal and dual objectives
certify optimality, Farkas multipliers certify infeasibility, and a feasible
point with an improving recession direction certifies unboundedness.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
Rational arithmetic is transferred exactly to the real interpretation.
Optimality uses weak duality; infeasibility uses certificate soundness;
unboundedness follows by taking arbitrarily large nonnegative multiples
of the certified recession direction. No solver or certificate-existence
theorem is needed to check a supplied certificate.

title: Soundness of exact rational LP certificates

Every valid rational certificate establishes its claimed outcome for the

namespace Lax109476.CertificateSoundness

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.RationalCertificates

/-- Exact rational certificate checks imply the asserted real LP outcome. -/
axiom valid_certificate_correct :
  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℚ m n) (certificate : Certificate m n),
    IsValidCertificate P certificate → IsCorrectOutcome P certificate

end Lax109476.CertificateSoundness

concepts.title: Polynomial-time certified optimization
concepts.description:
One polynomial-time word-RAM algorithm returns an exact certificate of the
correct real outcome for every rational linear program: optimality,
infeasibility, or unboundedness.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
This combines the exact solver specification with certificate soundness.
The output equals the encoding of a certificate that both passes the exact

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.RationalEncoding

/-!
---
title: Polynomial-time certified optimization
type: theorem
---
One polynomial-time word-RAM algorithm returns an exact certificate of the
correct real outcome for every rational linear program: optimality,
infeasibility, or unboundedness.

# Formalization notes

This combines the exact solver specification with certificate soundness.
The output equals the encoding of a certificate that both passes the exact
rational conditions and establishes the corresponding claim over real
variables. The two guarantees refer to the same certificate.
-/

namespace Lax109476.CertifiedOptimization

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.RationalCertificates Lax109476.RationalEncoding
open Lax759944.RamPolytime

/-- A uniform polynomial-time RAM returns valid certificates of the real outcome. -/
axiom exists_certified_polynomial_time_solver :
  ∃ solve : List ℕ → List ℕ, RamPolytime solve ∧
    ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℚ m n), ∃ certificate : Certificate m n,
      solve (encodeProgram P) = encodeCertificate certificate ∧
        IsValidCertificate P certificate ∧ IsCorrectOutcome P certificate

end Lax109476.CertifiedOptimization

statements.signature:
exists_certified_polynomial_time_solver : Exists fun solve =>
  And (Lax759944.RamPolytime.RamPolytime solve)
    (∀ (m n : Nat) (P : Lax109476.LinearProgram.Program Rat m n),
      Exists fun certificate =>
        And
          (Eq (solve (Lax109476.RationalEncoding.encodeProgram P))
            (Lax109476.RationalEncoding.encodeCertificate certificate))
          (And (Lax109476.RationalCertificates.IsValidCertificate P certificate)
            (Lax109476.RationalCertificates.IsCorrectOutcome P certificate)))
statements.doc: A uniform polynomial-time RAM returns valid certificates of the real outcome.

concepts.title: Complementary slackness
concepts.description:
For a primal feasible point $x$ and a dual feasible point $y$, the objective
values agree if and only if
$$y_i(b_i-(Ax)_i)=0\quad\text{for every }i,$$
$$x_j((A^T y)_j-c_j)=0\quad\text{for every }j.$$
Thus matching feasible certificates can equivalently be checked by these
complementarity conditions.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
Feasibility makes every displayed product nonnegative. The difference of
the objectives is the sum of all these products, so it vanishes exactly
when each product vanishes. This identity requires no existence theorem.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-!
---
title: Complementary slackness
type: theorem
---
For a primal feasible point $x$ and a dual feasible point $y$, the objective
values agree if and only if
$$y_i(b_i-(Ax)_i)=0\quad\text{for every }i,$$
$$x_j((A^T y)_j-c_j)=0\quad\text{for every }j.$$
Thus matching feasible certificates can equivalently be checked by these
complementarity conditions.

# Formalization notes

Feasibility makes every displayed product nonnegative. The difference of
the objectives is the sum of all these products, so it vanishes exactly
when each product vanishes. This identity requires no existence theorem.
-/

namespace Lax109476.ComplementarySlackness

open Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-- Matching feasible objectives are equivalent to coordinatewise complementarity. -/
axiom matching_iff_slackness :
  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℝ m n) (x : Fin n → ℝ) (y : Fin m → ℝ),
    PrimalFeasible P x → DualFeasible P y →
      (primalValue P x = dualValue P y ↔
        (∀ i, y i * (P.b i - rowValue P x i) = 0) ∧
        (∀ j, x j * (columnValue P y j - P.c j) = 0))

end Lax109476.ComplementarySlackness

statements.signature:
matching_iff_slackness : ∀ (m n : Nat) (P : Lax109476.LinearProgram.Program Real m n) (x : Fin n → Real) (y : Fin m → Real),
  Lax109476.LinearProgram.PrimalFeasible P x →
    Lax109476.LinearProgram.DualFeasible P y →
      Iff (Eq (Lax109476.LinearProgram.primalValue P x) (Lax109476.LinearProgram.dualValue P y))
        (And
          (∀ (i : Fin m), Eq (instHMul.hMul (y i) (instHSub.hSub (P.b i) (Lax109476.LinearProgram.rowValue P x i))) 0)
          (∀ (j : Fin n),
            Eq (instHMul.hMul (x j) (instHSub.hSub (Lax109476.LinearProgram.columnValue P y j) (P.c j))) 0))
statements.doc: Matching feasible objectives are equivalent to coordinatewise complementarity.

concepts.title: The feasibility alternative
concepts.description:
A real system $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$ is infeasible if and only if there is a
vector $y\ge0$ with $A^T y\ge0$ and $b^T y<0$.

This packages the existence and soundness directions as an equivalence.
Its proof assumes Farkas' lemma and the separately proved soundness of
infeasibility certificates.

import Lax109476.FarkasCertificate

/-!
---
title: The feasibility alternative
type: theorem
---
A real system $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$ is infeasible if and only if there is a
vector $y\ge0$ with $A^T y\ge0$ and $b^T y<0$.

# Formalization notes

This packages the existence and soundness directions as an equivalence.
Its proof assumes Farkas' lemma and the separately proved soundness of
infeasibility certificates.
-/

namespace Lax109476.FarkasAlternative

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.FarkasCertificate

/-- Infeasibility is equivalent to the existence of separating row multipliers. -/
axiom infeasible_iff_certificate :
  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℝ m n),
    ¬ IsFeasible P ↔ ∃ y : Fin m → ℝ, IsInfeasibilityCertificate P y

end Lax109476.FarkasAlternative

statements.signature:
infeasible_iff_certificate : ∀ (m n : Nat) (P : Lax109476.LinearProgram.Program Real m n),
  Iff (Not (Lax109476.LinearProgram.IsFeasible P))
    (Exists fun y => Lax109476.FarkasCertificate.IsInfeasibilityCertificate P y)
statements.doc: Infeasibility is equivalent to the existence of separating row multipliers.

concepts.title: Certificates of infeasibility
concepts.description:
For the system $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$, an infeasibility certificate is a vector
$y$ satisfying
$$y\ge0,\qquad A^T y\ge0,\qquad b^T y<0.$$
Such a vector is incompatible with primal feasibility: multiplying the
constraints by $y$ would give $0\le y^T Ax\le y^T b<0$.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The certificate is defined over the same coefficient field as the program,
so rational certificates can be checked exactly. The objective coefficients
are irrelevant to this certificate. Existence of a certificate for every
infeasible real system is the separate Farkas theorem.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-!
---
title: Certificates of infeasibility
type: definition
---
For the system $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$, an infeasibility certificate is a vector
$y$ satisfying
$$y\ge0,\qquad A^T y\ge0,\qquad b^T y<0.$$
Such a vector is incompatible with primal feasibility: multiplying the
constraints by $y$ would give $0\le y^T Ax\le y^T b<0$.

# Formalization notes

The certificate is defined over the same coefficient field as the program,
so rational certificates can be checked exactly. The objective coefficients
are irrelevant to this certificate. Existence of a certificate for every
infeasible real system is the separate Farkas theorem.
-/

namespace Lax109476.FarkasCertificate

open Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-- Nonnegative row multipliers certify an impossible negative upper bound. -/
def IsInfeasibilityCertificate {K : Type} [Ring K] [PartialOrder K] {m n : ℕ}
    (P : Program K m n) (y : Fin m → K) : Prop :=
  (∀ i, 0 ≤ y i) ∧ (∀ j, 0 ≤ columnValue P y j) ∧ dualValue P y < 0

end Lax109476.FarkasCertificate

concepts.title: Farkas' lemma
concepts.description:
If $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$ has no solution, there is a certificate
$$y\ge0,\qquad A^T y\ge0,\qquad b^T y<0.$$
Together with certificate soundness, this is the alternative between
feasibility and a certificate of infeasibility.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
This is the inequality form of Farkas' lemma. We state the existence
direction separately from the elementary soundness argument. Coefficients
and witnesses are real; exact rational certificates are treated downstream.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.FarkasCertificate

/-!
---
title: Farkas' lemma
type: theorem
---
If $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$ has no solution, there is a certificate
$$y\ge0,\qquad A^T y\ge0,\qquad b^T y<0.$$
Together with certificate soundness, this is the alternative between
feasibility and a certificate of infeasibility.

# Formalization notes

This is the inequality form of Farkas' lemma. We state the existence
direction separately from the elementary soundness argument. Coefficients
and witnesses are real; exact rational certificates are treated downstream.
-/

namespace Lax109476.FarkasLemma

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.FarkasCertificate

/-- Every infeasible real system has nonnegative separating multipliers. -/
axiom exists_infeasibility_certificate :
  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℝ m n), ¬ IsFeasible P →
    ∃ y : Fin m → ℝ, IsInfeasibilityCertificate P y

end Lax109476.FarkasLemma

statements.signature:
exists_infeasibility_certificate : ∀ (m n : Nat) (P : Lax109476.LinearProgram.Program Real m n),
  Not (Lax109476.LinearProgram.IsFeasible P) →
    Exists fun y => Lax109476.FarkasCertificate.IsInfeasibilityCertificate P y
statements.doc: Every infeasible real system has nonnegative separating multipliers.

concepts.title: Soundness of infeasibility certificates
concepts.description:
If $y\ge0$, $A^T y\ge0$, and $b^T y<0$, the system $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$
has no solution. This is the elementary soundness direction of the
alternative expressed by Farkas' lemma.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The proof rearranges finite sums and uses nonnegative multipliers. It
does not assume the existence direction of Farkas' lemma.

title: Soundness of infeasibility certificates
type: theorem

If $y\ge0$, $A^T y\ge0$, and $b^T y<0$, the system $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$

The proof rearranges finite sums and uses nonnegative multipliers. It

namespace Lax109476.FarkasSoundness

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.FarkasCertificate

/-- A negative certified upper bound is incompatible with primal feasibility. -/
axiom certificate_not_feasible :
  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℝ m n) (y : Fin m → ℝ),
    IsInfeasibilityCertificate P y → ¬ IsFeasible P

end Lax109476.FarkasSoundness

concepts.title: Fourier–Motzkin elimination
concepts.description:
One variable can be eliminated from a finite system of real linear
inequalities by nonnegative combinations of its rows. Pair each row with
positive coefficient of the eliminated variable with each row with negative
coefficient, and retain the rows with zero coefficient. The resulting finite
system is feasible exactly when the original system is feasible.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The variables in this elimination step are unrestricted. Nonnegative
variables are represented by additional inequalities when deriving Farkas'
lemma. The matrix $M$ gives the nonnegative row combinations. Its last
column in $MA$ is zero, and the remaining columns describe the reduced
system. This is an algebraic elimination theorem, with no polynomial-time
claim: repeated elimination may produce exponentially many inequalities.

concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib.Data.Matrix.Mul
import Mathlib.Data.Real.Basic

/-!
---
title: Fourier–Motzkin elimination
type: theorem
---
One variable can be eliminated from a finite system of real linear
inequalities by nonnegative combinations of its rows. Pair each row with
positive coefficient of the eliminated variable with each row with negative
coefficient, and retain the rows with zero coefficient. The resulting finite
system is feasible exactly when the original system is feasible.

# Formalization notes

The variables in this elimination step are unrestricted. Nonnegative
variables are represented by additional inequalities when deriving Farkas'
lemma. The matrix $M$ gives the nonnegative row combinations. Its last
column in $MA$ is zero, and the remaining columns describe the reduced
system. This is an algebraic elimination theorem, with no polynomial-time
claim: repeated elimination may produce exponentially many inequalities.
-/

namespace Lax109476.FourierMotzkin

/-- Eliminate the last variable using nonnegative row combinations. -/
axiom exists_elimination :
  ∀ (m : Type) [Fintype m] (n : ℕ)
    (A : Matrix m (Fin (n + 1)) ℝ) (b : m → ℝ),
    ∃ κ : Type, ∃ _ : Fintype κ, ∃ M : Matrix κ m ℝ,
      (∀ i j, 0 ≤ M i j) ∧
      (∀ i, (M * A) i (Fin.last n) = 0) ∧
      ((∃ x : Fin (n + 1) → ℝ, A.mulVec x ≤ b) ↔
        ∃ x' : Fin n → ℝ,
          (M * (A.submatrix id Fin.castSucc)).mulVec x' ≤ M.mulVec b)

end Lax109476.FourierMotzkin

statements.signature:
exists_elimination : ∀ (m : Type) [inst : Fintype m] (n : Nat) (A : Matrix m (Fin (instHAdd.hAdd n 1)) Real) (b : m → Real),
  Exists fun κ =>
    Exists fun x =>
      Exists fun M =>
        And (∀ (i : κ) (j : m), Real.instLE.le 0 (M i j))
          (And (∀ (i : κ), Eq (Matrix.instHMulOfFintypeOfMulOfAddCommMonoid.hMul M A i (Fin.last n)) 0)
            (Iff (Exists fun x => Pi.hasLe.le (A.mulVec x) b)
              (Exists fun x' =>
                Pi.hasLe.le
                  ((Matrix.instHMulOfFintypeOfMulOfAddCommMonoid.hMul M (A.submatrix id Fin.castSucc)).mulVec x')
                  (M.mulVec b))))
statements.doc: Eliminate the last variable using nonnegative row combinations.

concepts.title: Linear programs and their duals
concepts.description:
A linear program in inequality form is
$$\max\{c^T x: Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}.$$
Its dual is
$$\min\{b^T y: A^T y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}.$$
All vector inequalities are componentwise. A feasible maximization program
is bounded above if one finite real number bounds the objective of every
feasible point. A primal point is optimal if it is feasible and no feasible
point has a larger objective.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
There are `n` variables and `m` inequalities, indexed by `Fin n` and `Fin m`.
The coefficient data are shared by real and rational instances. Feasibility
and objective formulas are the same in either field. Both dimensions may be
zero. No feasibility, boundedness, optimizer, or optimum value is bundled
into the input data. Theorems state the necessary hypotheses explicitly.
Equality constraints and unrestricted variables can be represented by paired
inequalities and differences of nonnegative variables.

concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib.Algebra.BigOperators.Ring.Finset
import Mathlib.Data.Real.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Basic

/-!
---
title: Linear programs and their duals
type: definition
---
A linear program in inequality form is
$$\max\{c^T x: Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}.$$
Its dual is
$$\min\{b^T y: A^T y\ge c,\ y\ge0\}.$$
All vector inequalities are componentwise. A feasible maximization program
is bounded above if one finite real number bounds the objective of every
feasible point. A primal point is optimal if it is feasible and no feasible
point has a larger objective.

# Formalization notes

There are `n` variables and `m` inequalities, indexed by `Fin n` and `Fin m`.
The coefficient data are shared by real and rational instances. Feasibility
and objective formulas are the same in either field. Both dimensions may be
zero. No feasibility, boundedness, optimizer, or optimum value is bundled
into the input data. Theorems state the necessary hypotheses explicitly.
Equality constraints and unrestricted variables can be represented by paired
inequalities and differences of nonnegative variables.
-/

open scoped BigOperators

namespace Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-- Coefficients of a maximization program with `m` inequalities and `n`
nonnegative variables. -/
structure Program (K : Type) (m n : ℕ) where
  /-- The constraint matrix. -/
  A : Fin m → Fin n → K
  /-- The upper bounds on the constraint rows. -/
  b : Fin m → K
  /-- The coefficients of the maximized objective. -/
  c : Fin n → K

/-- The value of one constraint row at a primal point. -/
def rowValue {K : Type} [Ring K] {m n : ℕ} (P : Program K m n)
    (x : Fin n → K) (i : Fin m) : K :=
  ∑ j, P.A i j * x j

/-- One component of the transposed matrix applied to a dual point. -/
def columnValue {K : Type} [Ring K] {m n : ℕ} (P : Program K m n)
    (y : Fin m → K) (j : Fin n) : K :=
  ∑ i, P.A i j * y i

/-- The primal objective value. -/
def primalValue {K : Type} [Ring K] {m n : ℕ} (P : Program K m n)
    (x : Fin n → K) : K :=
  ∑ j, P.c j * x j

/-- The dual objective value. -/
def dualValue {K : Type} [Ring K] {m n : ℕ} (P : Program K m n)
    (y : Fin m → K) : K :=
  ∑ i, P.b i * y i

/-- A nonnegative primal point satisfies all row upper bounds. -/
def PrimalFeasible {K : Type} [Ring K] [PartialOrder K] {m n : ℕ}
    (P : Program K m n) (x : Fin n → K) : Prop :=
  (∀ j, 0 ≤ x j) ∧ ∀ i, rowValue P x i ≤ P.b i

/-- A nonnegative dual point dominates every objective coefficient. -/
def DualFeasible {K : Type} [Ring K] [PartialOrder K] {m n : ℕ}
    (P : Program K m n) (y : Fin m → K) : Prop :=
  (∀ i, 0 ≤ y i) ∧ ∀ j, P.c j ≤ columnValue P y j

/-- The real primal feasible set is nonempty. -/
def IsFeasible {m n : ℕ} (P : Program ℝ m n) : Prop :=
  ∃ x, PrimalFeasible P x

/-- A finite upper bound holds for every real primal feasible point. -/
def IsBoundedAbove {m n : ℕ} (P : Program ℝ m n) : Prop :=
  ∃ B : ℝ, ∀ x, PrimalFeasible P x → primalValue P x ≤ B

/-- A primal feasible point maximizes the objective over the feasible set. -/
def IsPrimalOptimal {K : Type} [Ring K] [PartialOrder K] {m n : ℕ}
    (P : Program K m n) (x : Fin n → K) : Prop :=
  PrimalFeasible P x ∧ ∀ z, PrimalFeasible P z → primalValue P z ≤ primalValue P x

end Lax109476.LinearProgram

concepts.title: Optimal dual multipliers
concepts.description:
Every optimal primal point $x$ of a real linear program has dual feasible
multipliers $y$ whose objective equals $c^T x$.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
This is the multiplier step in strong duality. Farkas' lemma is applied to
the system $y\ge0$, $A^T y\ge c$, $b^T y\le c^T x$. If that system
were infeasible, its certificate would produce either a better primal
point or a direction improving the objective, contradicting optimality.
Weak duality turns the final upper-bound inequality into equality.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-!
---
title: Optimal dual multipliers
type: theorem
---
Every optimal primal point $x$ of a real linear program has dual feasible
multipliers $y$ whose objective equals $c^T x$.

# Formalization notes

This is the multiplier step in strong duality. Farkas' lemma is applied to
the system $y\ge0$, $A^T y\ge c$, $b^T y\le c^T x$. If that system
were infeasible, its certificate would produce either a better primal
point or a direction improving the objective, contradicting optimality.
Weak duality turns the final upper-bound inequality into equality.
-/

namespace Lax109476.OptimalDualMultipliers

open Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-- An attained primal optimum has a matching feasible dual certificate. -/
axiom exists_matching_dual :
  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℝ m n) (x : Fin n → ℝ), IsPrimalOptimal P x →
    ∃ y : Fin m → ℝ, DualFeasible P y ∧ primalValue P x = dualValue P y

end Lax109476.OptimalDualMultipliers

statements.signature:
exists_matching_dual : ∀ (m n : Nat) (P : Lax109476.LinearProgram.Program Real m n) (x : Fin n → Real),
  Lax109476.LinearProgram.IsPrimalOptimal P x →
    Exists fun y =>
      And (Lax109476.LinearProgram.DualFeasible P y)
        (Eq (Lax109476.LinearProgram.primalValue P x) (Lax109476.LinearProgram.dualValue P y))
statements.doc: An attained primal optimum has a matching feasible dual certificate.

concepts.title: Exact polynomial-time linear programming on a word RAM
concepts.description:
There is one polynomial-time word-RAM algorithm that solves every rational
linear program exactly. It returns either an optimal primal point and matching
dual multipliers, an infeasibility certificate, or a feasible point and an
improving recession direction certifying unboundedness.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
This is the classical polynomial-time solvability theorem for rational
linear programming, with the outcomes stated through exact certificates.
The computation predicate is `Lax759944.RamPolytime.RamPolytime`, using the
registered word RAM and the input's binary size. The returned word must
equal the encoding of the same certificate whose conditions are checked.
No fixed dimension, bounded coefficient magnitude, or feasibility promise
is imposed. Empty dimensions are included.

The existence of a polynomial-time solver is the algorithmic obligation;
ellipsoid-method internals are not separate claims in this submission.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.RationalEncoding

/-!
---
title: Exact polynomial-time linear programming on a word RAM
type: theorem
---
There is one polynomial-time word-RAM algorithm that solves every rational
linear program exactly. It returns either an optimal primal point and matching
dual multipliers, an infeasibility certificate, or a feasible point and an
improving recession direction certifying unboundedness.

# Formalization notes

This is the classical polynomial-time solvability theorem for rational
linear programming, with the outcomes stated through exact certificates.
The computation predicate is `Lax759944.RamPolytime.RamPolytime`, using the
registered word RAM and the input's binary size. The returned word must
equal the encoding of the same certificate whose conditions are checked.
No fixed dimension, bounded coefficient magnitude, or feasibility promise
is imposed. Empty dimensions are included.

The existence of a polynomial-time solver is the algorithmic obligation;
ellipsoid-method internals are not separate claims in this submission.
-/

namespace Lax109476.PolynomialTimeSolver

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.RationalCertificates Lax109476.RationalEncoding
open Lax759944.RamPolytime

/-- One uniform polynomial-time RAM produces exact certificates for every LP. -/
axiom exists_exact_polynomial_time_solver :
  ∃ solve : List ℕ → List ℕ, RamPolytime solve ∧
    ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℚ m n), ∃ certificate : Certificate m n,
      solve (encodeProgram P) = encodeCertificate certificate ∧
        IsValidCertificate P certificate

end Lax109476.PolynomialTimeSolver

statements.signature:
exists_exact_polynomial_time_solver : Exists fun solve =>
  And (Lax759944.RamPolytime.RamPolytime solve)
    (∀ (m n : Nat) (P : Lax109476.LinearProgram.Program Rat m n),
      Exists fun certificate =>
        And
          (Eq (solve (Lax109476.RationalEncoding.encodeProgram P))
            (Lax109476.RationalEncoding.encodeCertificate certificate))
          (Lax109476.RationalCertificates.IsValidCertificate P certificate))
statements.doc: One uniform polynomial-time RAM produces exact certificates for every LP.

concepts.title: Attainment of a finite linear-programming optimum
concepts.description:
If a real linear program is feasible and its objective is bounded above on
the feasible set, it attains its maximum at a feasible point.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
No compactness assumption is imposed on the feasible polyhedron. Linear
objectives attain their finite optima on nonempty polyhedra even when those
polyhedra are unbounded. This is the attainment step used with Farkas'
lemma to obtain an optimal dual certificate. The supplied proof applies Farkas'
lemma to the original system with an objective threshold equal to the finite
supremum; a separating certificate would contradict feasibility or produce
a strictly smaller dual upper bound.

concepts.title: Exact rational solution certificates
concepts.description:
A rational linear program is a linear program with rational coefficients,
still optimized over real variables. Its outcomes have three certificate forms:

* an optimal primal point and matching dual multipliers;
* nonnegative Farkas multipliers certifying infeasibility;
* a feasible primal point and an improving recession direction certifying
  unboundedness.

Every coordinate in these certificates is rational, and all certificate
conditions can be checked by exact rational arithmetic.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The three constructors carry precisely the witnesses needed for their
claims. The predicates use the same row, column, and objective formulas
as the real program. The real interpretation casts the coefficient data
and witness coordinates exactly. No outcome or correctness proof is
assumed as part of the input.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.FarkasCertificate
import Lax109476.RecessionDirection
import Mathlib.Data.Rat.Cast.Order

/-!
---
title: Exact rational solution certificates
type: definition
---
A rational linear program is a linear program with rational coefficients,
still optimized over real variables. Its outcomes have three certificate forms:

* an optimal primal point and matching dual multipliers;
* nonnegative Farkas multipliers certifying infeasibility;
* a feasible primal point and an improving recession direction certifying
  unboundedness.

Every coordinate in these certificates is rational, and all certificate
conditions can be checked by exact rational arithmetic.

# Formalization notes

The three constructors carry precisely the witnesses needed for their
claims. The predicates use the same row, column, and objective formulas
as the real program. The real interpretation casts the coefficient data
and witness coordinates exactly. No outcome or correctness proof is
assumed as part of the input.
-/

namespace Lax109476.RationalCertificates

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.FarkasCertificate Lax109476.RecessionDirection

/-- Interpret rational coefficient data as a real linear program. -/
def toReal {m n : ℕ} (P : Program ℚ m n) : Program ℝ m n where
  A i j := P.A i j
  b i := P.b i
  c j := P.c j

/-- The exact real interpretation of a rational vector. -/
def realVector {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → ℚ) : Fin n → ℝ := fun j => x j

/-- A rational certificate for one of the three possible LP outcomes. -/
inductive Certificate (m n : ℕ)
  /-- Primal and dual points with matching objectives. -/
  | optimal (x : Fin n → ℚ) (y : Fin m → ℚ)
  /-- Separating nonnegative multipliers for an infeasible primal system. -/
  | infeasible (y : Fin m → ℚ)
  /-- A feasible base point and an improving recession direction. -/
  | unbounded (x d : Fin n → ℚ)

/-- The exact rational inequalities and equalities validating a certificate. -/
def IsValidCertificate {m n : ℕ} (P : Program ℚ m n) : Certificate m n → Prop
  | .optimal x y => PrimalFeasible P x ∧ DualFeasible P y ∧ primalValue P x = dualValue P y
  | .infeasible y => IsInfeasibilityCertificate P y
  | .unbounded x d => PrimalFeasible P x ∧ IsImprovingDirection P d

/-- The real mathematical claim made by each certificate constructor. -/
def IsCorrectOutcome {m n : ℕ} (P : Program ℚ m n) : Certificate m n → Prop
  | .optimal x _ => IsPrimalOptimal (toReal P) (realVector x)
  | .infeasible _ => ¬ IsFeasible (toReal P)
  | .unbounded _ _ => IsFeasible (toReal P) ∧ ¬ IsBoundedAbove (toReal P)

end Lax109476.RationalCertificates

concepts.title: Binary-size encoding of rational linear programs
concepts.description:
An LP input word begins with its number of inequalities $m$ and variables
$n$, followed by the matrix in row order, the vector $b$, and the vector $c$.
A rational is encoded by its numerator sign, numerator magnitude, and
positive denominator, in reduced form. Solution words begin with an outcome
tag and contain the corresponding rational certificate coordinates.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The input sign is zero for nonnegative numerators and one for negative
numerators. Output tags zero, one, and two mean optimal, infeasible, and
unbounded. Dimensions are supplied by the input, so witness vectors have
fixed known lengths. Each rational keeps its exact denominator.

The imported `RamPolytime` predicate uses binary word-list size, a single
uniform program, polynomial bounds on sufficient word length and executed
instructions, and correctness at every sufficiently large word length on
Lax808846's registered RAM. Its specified physical tape is length-prefixed.
Malformed logical inputs have no prescribed output, but the solver function
is total. No new machine model or abstract running-time annotation is introduced.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.RationalCertificates
import Lax759944.RamPolytime

/-!
---
title: Binary-size encoding of rational linear programs
type: definition
---
An LP input word begins with its number of inequalities $m$ and variables
$n$, followed by the matrix in row order, the vector $b$, and the vector $c$.
A rational is encoded by its numerator sign, numerator magnitude, and
positive denominator, in reduced form. Solution words begin with an outcome
tag and contain the corresponding rational certificate coordinates.

# Formalization notes

The input sign is zero for nonnegative numerators and one for negative
numerators. Output tags zero, one, and two mean optimal, infeasible, and
unbounded. Dimensions are supplied by the input, so witness vectors have
fixed known lengths. Each rational keeps its exact denominator.

The imported `RamPolytime` predicate uses binary word-list size, a single
uniform program, polynomial bounds on sufficient word length and executed
instructions, and correctness at every sufficiently large word length on
Lax808846's registered RAM. Its specified physical tape is length-prefixed.
Malformed logical inputs have no prescribed output, but the solver function
is total. No new machine model or abstract running-time annotation is introduced.
-/

namespace Lax109476.RationalEncoding

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.RationalCertificates

/-- Encode a reduced rational by sign, magnitude, and denominator. -/
def encodeRational (q : ℚ) : List ℕ :=
  [if q.num < 0 then 1 else 0, q.num.natAbs, q.den]

/-- Encode all coordinates of a rational vector in index order. -/
def encodeVector {n : ℕ} (x : Fin n → ℚ) : List ℕ :=
  (List.ofFn x).flatMap encodeRational

/-- Encode dimensions, row-major coefficients, row bounds, and objective. -/
def encodeProgram {m n : ℕ} (P : Program ℚ m n) : List ℕ :=
  [m, n] ++ (List.ofFn fun i => List.ofFn (P.A i)).flatten.flatMap encodeRational ++
    encodeVector P.b ++ encodeVector P.c

/-- Encode the outcome tag and all rational certificate coordinates. -/
def encodeCertificate {m n : ℕ} : Certificate m n → List ℕ
  | .optimal x y => [0] ++ encodeVector x ++ encodeVector y
  | .infeasible y => [1] ++ encodeVector y
  | .unbounded x d => [2] ++ encodeVector x ++ encodeVector d

end Lax109476.RationalEncoding

concepts.title: Real feasibility of rational linear programs has a rational witness
concepts.description:
A finite linear system with rational coefficients has a nonnegative real
feasible point if and only if it has a nonnegative rational feasible point.
The direction requiring a rational witness follows from elimination over
the rationals and the soundness of rational infeasibility certificates over
the reals.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The statement imposes no full-dimension or interior-point condition. It
does not bound the size of the rational point or the time needed to find it.

  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℚ m n), IsFeasible (toReal P) →

concepts.title: Certificates of unboundedness
concepts.description:
An improving recession direction satisfies
$$d\ge0,\qquad Ad\le0,\qquad c^T d>0.$$
Together with any primal feasible point $x$, it certifies unboundedness:
$x+td$ is feasible for every $t\ge0$ and its objective tends to infinity.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
A direction alone does not certify that the primal is unbounded: the
feasible set could be empty. Certificates therefore include a feasible
base point as well as the direction.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-!
---
title: Certificates of unboundedness
type: definition
---
An improving recession direction satisfies
$$d\ge0,\qquad Ad\le0,\qquad c^T d>0.$$
Together with any primal feasible point $x$, it certifies unboundedness:
$x+td$ is feasible for every $t\ge0$ and its objective tends to infinity.

# Formalization notes

A direction alone does not certify that the primal is unbounded: the
feasible set could be empty. Certificates therefore include a feasible
base point as well as the direction.
-/

namespace Lax109476.RecessionDirection

open Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-- A nonnegative direction preserves every upper constraint and improves
the maximized objective. -/
def IsImprovingDirection {K : Type} [Ring K] [PartialOrder K] {m n : ℕ}
    (P : Program K m n) (d : Fin n → K) : Prop :=
  (∀ j, 0 ≤ d j) ∧ (∀ i, rowValue P d i ≤ 0) ∧ 0 < primalValue P d

end Lax109476.RecessionDirection

concepts.title: Unbounded linear programs have improving recession directions
concepts.description:
If the feasible objective values are unbounded above, there is a nonnegative
direction $d$ satisfying $Ad\le0$ and $c^Td>0$. Thus unboundedness has a
geometric witness, in addition to the soundness of such witnesses.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The coefficients and direction are real. This theorem does not give rational
encoding bounds or an algorithm for recovering the direction. Empty dimensions
are included.

/-!
---
title: Unbounded linear programs have improving recession directions
type: theorem
---
If the feasible objective values are unbounded above, there is a nonnegative
direction $d$ satisfying $Ad\le0$ and $c^Td>0$. Thus unboundedness has a
geometric witness, in addition to the soundness of such witnesses.

namespace Lax109476.RecessionExistence

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.RecessionDirection

/-- Unbounded feasible objective values force an improving recession direction. -/
axiom exists_improving_direction :
  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℝ m n), ¬ IsBoundedAbove P →
    ∃ d : Fin n → ℝ, IsImprovingDirection P d

end Lax109476.RecessionExistence

  Not (Lax109476.LinearProgram.IsBoundedAbove P) → Exists fun d => Lax109476.RecessionDirection.IsImprovingDirection P d

concepts.title: Improving directions certify unboundedness
concepts.description:
A feasible point $x$ and an improving recession direction $d$ certify that
the objective is unbounded above. For every $t\ge0$, the point $x+td$ is
feasible and has objective $c^T x+t c^T d$, which tends to infinity.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The feasible base point is essential: an improving direction by itself
does not imply that the program has any feasible points. This is certificate
soundness and does not assert existence of a rational recession certificate.

concepts.title: Polynomial-size rational LP certificates
concepts.description:
Every rational linear program has a valid outcome certificate whose total
binary encoding size is polynomial in the binary encoding size of the input.
The polynomial is universal over all dimensions and coefficient values.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The statement includes all three outcomes, and thus also asserts the
existence of exact rational witnesses. The size counts signs, numerators,
denominators, and outcome data in the fixed word-list encoding. The proof
clears input denominators, compresses each certificate using independent
supports, and applies Cramer's rule to an integer Gram matrix. The resulting
certificate encoding has size at most $512(L+1)^3$, where $L$ is the input
encoding size. It uses rational certificate existence and does not depend on
the algorithm or its running-time theorem.

/-!
---
title: Polynomial-size rational LP certificates
type: theorem
---
Every rational linear program has a valid outcome certificate whose total
binary encoding size is polynomial in the binary encoding size of the input.
The polynomial is universal over all dimensions and coefficient values.

# Formalization notes

The statement includes all three outcomes, and thus also asserts the
existence of exact rational witnesses. The size counts signs, numerators,
denominators, and outcome data in the fixed word-list encoding. The proof
clears input denominators, compresses each certificate using independent
supports, and applies Cramer's rule to an integer Gram matrix. The resulting

namespace Lax109476.SmallCertificates

open Lax109476.LinearProgram Lax109476.RationalCertificates Lax109476.RationalEncoding
open Lax759944.BinaryWordEncoding

/-- All rational LP outcomes have certificates of uniformly polynomial bit size. -/
axiom exists_polynomial_size_certificate :
  ∃ C k : ℕ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℚ m n),
    ∃ certificate : Certificate m n, IsValidCertificate P certificate ∧
      bitSize (encodeCertificate certificate) ≤ C * (bitSize (encodeProgram P) + 1) ^ k

end Lax109476.SmallCertificates

statements.signature:
exists_polynomial_size_certificate : Exists fun C =>
  Exists fun k =>
    And (instLTNat.lt 0 C)
      (∀ (m n : Nat) (P : Lax109476.LinearProgram.Program Rat m n),
        Exists fun certificate =>
          And (Lax109476.RationalCertificates.IsValidCertificate P certificate)
            (instLENat.le
              (Lax759944.BinaryWordEncoding.bitSize (Lax109476.RationalEncoding.encodeCertificate certificate))
              (instHMul.hMul C
                (instHPow.hPow
                  (instHAdd.hAdd (Lax759944.BinaryWordEncoding.bitSize (Lax109476.RationalEncoding.encodeProgram P)) 1)
                  k))))
statements.doc: All rational LP outcomes have certificates of uniformly polynomial bit size.

concepts.title: Strong duality
concepts.description:
If a real primal linear program is feasible and bounded above, there are
primal and dual feasible points $x,y$ with equal objective values:
$$c^T x=b^T y.$$
By weak duality, these points are optimal for their respective programs.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The statement includes attainment on both sides and requires no strict
feasibility or interior-point hypothesis. The proof network separates
primal attainment from the construction of optimal dual multipliers by
Farkas' lemma.

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-!
---
title: Strong duality
type: theorem
---
If a real primal linear program is feasible and bounded above, there are
primal and dual feasible points $x,y$ with equal objective values:
$$c^T x=b^T y.$$
By weak duality, these points are optimal for their respective programs.

# Formalization notes

The statement includes attainment on both sides and requires no strict
feasibility or interior-point hypothesis. The proof network separates
primal attainment from the construction of optimal dual multipliers by
Farkas' lemma.
-/

namespace Lax109476.StrongDuality

open Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-- A feasible bounded real program has matching primal and dual optimizers. -/
axiom exists_matching_optimizers :
  ∀ (m n : ℕ) (P : Program ℝ m n), IsFeasible P → IsBoundedAbove P →
    ∃ (x : Fin n → ℝ) (y : Fin m → ℝ),
      PrimalFeasible P x ∧ DualFeasible P y ∧ primalValue P x = dualValue P y

end Lax109476.StrongDuality

statements.signature:
exists_matching_optimizers : ∀ (m n : Nat) (P : Lax109476.LinearProgram.Program Real m n),
  Lax109476.LinearProgram.IsFeasible P →
    Lax109476.LinearProgram.IsBoundedAbove P →
      Exists fun x =>
        Exists fun y =>
          And (Lax109476.LinearProgram.PrimalFeasible P x)
            (And (Lax109476.LinearProgram.DualFeasible P y)
              (Eq (Lax109476.LinearProgram.primalValue P x) (Lax109476.LinearProgram.dualValue P y)))
statements.doc: A feasible bounded real program has matching primal and dual optimizers.

concepts.title: Weak duality
concepts.description:
Every primal feasible point $x$ and dual feasible point $y$ satisfy
$$c^T x\le b^T y.$$
Thus a dual feasible point certifies an upper bound on the primal optimum.
If their objective values agree, both are optimal.

sections.title: Formalization notes
sections.markdown:
The statement uses arbitrary real coefficient data and does not require
either feasible set to be bounded. The proof is finite sum rearrangement
and multiplication of inequalities by nonnegative coordinates.

namespace Lax109476.WeakDuality

open Lax109476.LinearProgram

/-- Every primal objective is bounded by every dual objective. -/
axiom primalValue_le_dualValue :

proofs.description:
Let $\alpha$ be the finite supremum of the feasible objectives. Apply
Farkas' lemma to the original system with the extra constraint
$c^T x\ge\alpha$. An infeasibility certificate has a nonnegative multiplier
$t$ for this extra row. If $t=0$, it contradicts original feasibility.
If $t>0$, divide the remaining multipliers by $t$ to obtain a dual feasible
point with objective strictly below $\alpha$. Weak duality then contradicts
the supremum property. Thus the threshold system is feasible and attains
$\alpha$.

Combine Farkas certificate existence with the independent soundness theorem.
The two assumptions supply the two directions of the alternative.

A feasible point and a Farkas certificate would give a nonnegative
bilinear sum bounded above by a strictly negative number. This proves
soundness directly, without assuming Farkas certificate existence.

Multiply each dual inequality by the corresponding nonnegative primal
coordinate, rearrange the finite double sum, and multiply each primal
inequality by the corresponding nonnegative dual coordinate.
No LP existence theorem is used.

Split on real feasibility and boundedness. An infeasible rational system has
rational Farkas multipliers by rational elimination. In the bounded feasible
case, strong duality makes the combined primal–dual system with equal
objectives real feasible; rational feasibility gives a rational matching pair.
In the unbounded case, rationalize both a feasible base point and a recession
direction normalized to objective increase at least one. No solver theorem
or complexity assumption is used.

Exact rational equalities and inequalities survive the embedding into the
reals. Weak duality proves optimality of a matching pair, Farkas soundness
proves infeasibility, and recession soundness proves unboundedness. Neither
certificate existence nor a solver is needed to verify an outcome.

Given a proposed bound $B$, move from the feasible base point along the
improving direction by $(B-c^T x)/(c^T d)+1$. This nonnegative step preserves
feasibility and gives objective $B+c^T d>B$.

Apply Farkas' lemma to the proposed dual multipliers with the additional
constraint $b^T y\le c^T x$. If this system is infeasible, its separating
vector consists of a nonnegative vector $d$ and scalar $\lambda$ satisfying
$Ad\le\lambda b$ and $c^T d>\lambda c^T x$.
For $\lambda>0$, the point $d/\lambda$ improves the alleged optimum.
For $\lambda=0$, the point $x+d$ improves it. Both are contradictions.
The system is therefore feasible, and weak duality gives equality.

Primal attainment supplies an optimizer; the optimal-dual-multipliers
theorem supplies matching dual multipliers. The graph keeps these two
independent steps visible.

Add the inequalities $-x_j\le0$ to the rows of $Ax\le b$ and apply the
unrestricted-variable alternative proved by induction with Fourier–Motzkin
elimination. Split its nonnegative multipliers into original-row and
nonnegativity-row components. The zero column equations give $A^T y\ge0$;
the negative weighted bound is exactly $b^T y<0$.

coefficient. Combine every positive row with every negative row using
nonnegative multipliers, and retain the zero rows. A finite family of

proofs.description:
Keep the exact solver's program, runtime bound, and returned certificate.
Apply certificate soundness to that same certificate. The solver theorem
is the algorithmic assumption; soundness supplies the real outcome guarantee.

The duality gap equals the sum of the nonnegative row and column
complementarity products. A finite sum of nonnegative real numbers
vanishes exactly when all its terms vanish.

One fixed structured command decodes arbitrary input, selects a feasible
certificate system using exact ellipsoid decisions, recovers a rational
point, and writes its certificate. Its polynomial bounds transfer through
the registered compiler and word-RAM model.

If there were no rational feasible point, Fourier–Motzkin elimination over
the rationals would supply rational Farkas multipliers. Casting them into
the reals gives an infeasibility certificate, contradicting the real
feasible point. This argument also applies to lower-dimensional feasible sets.

Apply Farkas' lemma to $Ad\le0$, $d\ge0$, $c^Td\ge1$. An infeasibility
certificate has a strictly positive multiplier $t$ on the final row. Dividing
the other multipliers by $t$ gives a dual feasible vector for the original
program. Weak duality then supplies a finite objective bound, a contradiction.

Start with a valid rational certificate. Clear all input denominators with
one positive multiplier, preserving certificate validity. Encode each outcome
as a nonnegative integer inequality system, normalizing strict separation or
improvement to magnitude at least one. Minimal-support conic representations
have independent columns; Cramer's rule on their Gram matrix bounds all
reduced coordinates. The actual input encoding bounds both the dimension and
the sum of denominator sizes. The resulting certificate encoding is at most
512 times the cube of input size plus one. No solver theorem is assumed.
